subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 60 minutes × 2 periods = 120 minutes
  Row 2: 50 minutes × 13 periods = 650 minutes
Total: 15 periods · 12h 50min

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.97): graphic organiser on elderly — paired and class discussion

periods.activity_title: Activating Prior Knowledge: The Elderly Among Us

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the chapter title and invites students to guess what 'Vitamin-M' might mean, collecting responses on the board without confirming. This brief activation surfaces assumptions about memory, aging, and family care.

Students individually complete the graphic organiser from Reflect and Respond (p.97), noting why we care for the elderly, what problems they face, possible reasons, and how we can help. Teacher circulates and prompts with follow-up probes.

Pairs share their organisers, then the class opens into a full discussion guided by the four prompts. Teacher records key points on the board, drawing out lived experiences and contrasting city versus small-town elderly life.
Teacher consolidates the discussion by noting recurring themes — dignity, independence, memory — that will thread through the story. Students note two personal takeaways in their exercise books.

periods.teacher_notes: The story opens with Ravi's mother wishing someone would invent a pill to improve old people's memories, overheard by Grandpa; use students' organiser entries to anticipate this irony before reading begins. A common pitfall is letting confident speakers dominate — use pair-share first so quieter students arrive at whole-class discussion with a prepared point. An unanchored vocabulary-preview task (Task II, p.98) is flagged here as useful self-study before the next reading sitting.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.102): four short-answer questions on Grandpa's move to the city

periods.activity_title: Reading Aloud and First Comprehension: Grandpa Arrives

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the key themes surfaced in the prior discussion — dignity, independence, memory — then announces that the class will now read the opening section of the story together.

Teacher reads aloud pp.97–102 at a measured pace, students following in their textbooks; teacher pauses at Grandpa's description of his small brick house, the garden accident, and his arrival at the city flat to allow students to visualise the scenes.

Students answer the four Check Your Understanding questions (p.102) in writing individually, then compare with a neighbour before brief whole-class verification. Teacher probes: why does Ravi's sympathy for Grandpa matter for what comes next?

Teacher sets the homework task — a written reflection on a family tradition passed down by an elderly relative (Reflect and Respond, p.97–98) — and explains the connection between personal memory and the story's themes.

periods.teacher_notes: The opening pages establish Grandpa's dignity and his resentment at being treated like a child after managing house and cooking alone for ten years since his wife's death; draw students' attention to these details as they drive all that follows. A pitfall is rushing the read-aloud past Grandpa's lyrical description of his small-town garden — that passage is the emotional core of his nostalgia and should be savoured. Students who have completed the vocabulary preview from Task II will decode 'pottering' and 'winced' without interruption.

homework.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.97–98): share a family tradition passed down by an elderly relative — written reflection, 4–6 sentences

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.106): flow chart of Grandpa's day out — seven blanks

periods.activity_title: Reading the Chase: Comedy, Dignity, and Ravi's Dilemma

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws on the comprehension established during the reading of pp.97–102, asking students to recall Ravi's emotional stance toward Grandpa before the day out begins. One or two students share; teacher frames the tension between loyalty to mother and respect for Grandpa.

Teacher reads aloud pp.102–106, pausing to annotate the comic misadventures — the elephant-bush crawl, the vendor women, the Ladies' Hairdressing Salon eviction — and asking guided questions: why does Ravi not simply walk beside Grandpa? Students track Grandpa's movements on a rough sketch in their notebooks.

Students complete the flow chart (Check Your Understanding, p.106) independently, filling in the seven blanks describing Grandpa's day out. Pairs check answers; teacher leads whole-class confirmation, probing the sequence for any misreadings.
Teacher invites a brief oral reflection: which comic episode did students find most effective and why? This seeds the analytical angle for the Critical Reflection work to follow.

periods.teacher_notes: The comedy of errors in this section — crouching behind an elephant-shaped bush, being evicted from a hairdressing salon — is humane rather than slapstick; guide students to see that Ravi's predicament is driven by genuine care for Grandpa's dignity, not incompetence. A common pitfall is reading the comic scenes too quickly; each mishap rewards a pause so students picture the setting. The questions on Ravi's emotional state after finding Grandpa (Task 5, p.107) are earmarked for the following sitting.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.107): three questions on Grandpa's safe return and Ravi's reaction
Check Your Understanding (p.109): three analytical questions on the birthday twist and gift symbolism

periods.activity_title: Story's Close: Gifts, Wit, and the Birthday Twist

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws on the chase episode covered earlier, asking: students predicted whether Ravi's mother would discover what happened — now they will find out. This activates curiosity before reading the conclusion.

Teacher reads aloud pp.107–109, pausing at Grandpa's cool remark about Ravi's disappearance, at Ravi's mother's assumption that Grandpa has forgotten Ravi's birthday, and at the reveal that it is Grandpa's own birthday and he always gives gifts. Students annotate key lines.

Students answer the three questions from Check Your Understanding (p.107) and the three from Check Your Understanding (p.109) in writing. Teacher circulates, prompting deeper engagement: what does The Best Detective Stories as a gift reveal about Grandpa's awareness of Ravi's surveillance?

Whole-class discussion on the closing irony: Grandpa suggests Ravi's mother needs Vitamin-M. Teacher asks students to articulate in one sentence the story's final stance on who really has the sharper mind. Responses recorded on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The birthday twist — Grandpa always gives gifts on his own birthday — encapsulates the story's humane argument that the elderly are often wiser and more generous than they are credited; this is the emotional payoff of all the earlier comedy. A pitfall is accepting superficial answers about Grandpa being 'kind'; press students to link the detective book gift to the specific wink at Ravi's amateur surveillance. The Critical Reflection extract tasks (Tasks 7 and 8) will deepen this reading in the next sitting.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.109–110): Extract 1 — five questions on Grandpa's nostalgia and the garden accident
Critical Reflection (p.110–111): Extract 2 — five questions on Grandpa's cool tone and birthday surprise

periods.activity_title: Critical Reflection: Close Reading Two Key Extracts

time_bands.activity: Teacher re-reads Extract 1 aloud ('Grandpa hated the noise and bustle…') and Extract 2 ('I had a quiet morning…'), asking students to listen for tone and word choice. Students underline one word in each extract that they find most revealing.

Students work through the five Critical Reflection questions for Extract 1 (p.109–110) individually, then compare with a partner. Teacher circulates, prompting: what is the difference between 'nostalgic' and 'regretful' as descriptors here? Why does Grandpa use the image of a falling leaf?

Students work through the five Critical Reflection questions for Extract 2 (p.110–111), including the true/false item on whether Grandpa forgot Ravi's birthday. Pairs share reasoning; teacher facilitates a brief class-wide discussion on Grandpa's tone — calm authority versus passive aggression.
Teacher draws together both extracts: how does Grandpa's language in each extract undercut the opening assumption that he has a failing memory? Students note one-sentence answers in their books.

periods.teacher_notes: Both extracts are rich in irony: Extract 1 shows Grandpa's eloquence about his lost home even as his family dismisses his capacity; Extract 2 shows him wielding wit and timing to expose Ravi without cruelty. Ensure students distinguish 'nostalgic' from 'wistful' — Grandpa's longing is active and specific (the mango tree, the silence), not vague. The eight extended analytical questions of Critical Reflection II (Task 9, p.111) are reserved for the following sitting where fuller writing time is available.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection II (p.111): eight analytical questions — character traits, memory evidence, detective argument, age bias

periods.activity_title: Critical Reflection II: Character, Theme, and Age Bias

time_bands.activity: Having explored the two extracts in a prior close-reading sitting, teacher now frames the eight extended questions of Critical Reflection II (p.111) as a character and theme study. Teacher reads each question aloud, briefly clarifying what depth of answer is expected.

Students write responses to questions 1–6 independently (evidence disproving Grandpa's failing memory; character traits of all three characters; Ravi's worry at the tea stall; the detective argument for and against; Grandpa's awareness of surveillance). Teacher circulates with targeted prompts.

Students complete questions 7 and 8 — who needs Vitamin-M and why; a personal example of age-based bias. Pairs exchange books and offer one improvement suggestion for specificity or evidence. Teacher collects two or three responses to discuss whole-class.

Teacher orchestrates a brief plenary: who in the class argued that Ravi's mother needs Vitamin-M? Who argued for another character? Hands are counted; teacher notes that the story leaves the question productively open.

periods.teacher_notes: Question 1 — disproving Grandpa's failing memory — is analytically demanding; prompt students to cite Grandpa's chess encyclopaedia knowledge and his precise birthday-gift tradition as evidence, both drawn from the story's conclusion. A pitfall is students treating 'characteristic traits' as synonyms; press for traits supported by specific action (e.g. Ravi is caring, evidenced by the covert surveillance despite its cost to him). The age-bias question (question 8) benefits from personal testimony — create a safe space for students to share observations without naming individuals from their own communities.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.112): classify movement and sound words; fill blanks in Detective Shankar passage
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.113): synonym puzzle — QUANDARY and PREDICAMENT for 'dilemma'

periods.activity_title: Movement Words, Sound Words, and Word Families

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads five or six words from the story aloud — 'pottering', 'thudded', 'shrieks', 'sprinting', 'whirr' — and asks students to mime or describe the action or sound each evokes. This embodied warm-up anchors the word-sorting task.

Students classify all twenty words from Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.112) into movement words and sound words in their notebooks. They then use appropriate words from their sorted lists to fill the ten blanks in the Detective Shankar passage. Pairs compare classifications.

Teacher draws attention to the word 'dilemma' from the story and writes the two synonym puzzles on the board: QU_ND_ _Y and PR_D_C_M_NT (p.113). Students solve individually, then confirm with a dictionary. Teacher discusses how 'quandary' and 'predicament' differ in register and intensity from 'dilemma'.

Teacher sets the homework — the four-column word table for six story words (p.113) — and models one row ('craftily': meaning, part of speech, synonym, antonym) together as a class so the format is clear.

periods.teacher_notes: The movement-and-sound vocabulary in 'Vitamin-M' is unusually rich and kinetic — words like 'zigzagging', 'darted', and 'trailing' carry the whole comedy-of-errors chase; help students see that the author's word choices create pace and slapstick rather than mere description. A common pitfall is students placing 'bustle' only in movement; note it can evoke both hurried movement and noisy activity, making it a productive borderline case for discussion. The word-table homework builds the dictionary-work habit that underpins Tasks III and IV.

homework.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.113): complete the four-column word table for craftily, dilemma, furious, boomed, humiliation, attire

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.113): match emotions/expressions to meanings — one meaning extra
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.114): underline prepositions in story phrases; fill six blanks in preposition passage
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (pp.114–116): interrogative sentence types and reported speech — four MCQ and six fill-in-the-blank

time_bands.activity: Students complete the matching task (p.113) — five expressions from the story (embarrassed, countered, flushed, stricken, gleam) matched to six meanings, one extra — individually, then whole-class verification. Teacher highlights how 'flushed' and 'stricken' are visible body-language words the author uses to convey Ravi's inner state.

Students underline prepositions in the four story phrases (p.114), then fill in the six blanks in the preposition passage using the given option sets. Teacher draws the class's attention to how directional prepositions ('across', 'behind', 'under') map exactly onto Ravi's covert movements through the story's physical spaces.

Teacher introduces the grammar note on interrogative sentence types and direct-to-reported speech transformation (pp.114–116). Students answer the four multiple-choice questions on sentence types, then convert the six-dialogue Arvind–Priya conversation into reported speech, attending to tense shifts and pronoun changes.

Teacher invites two students to read their reported-speech sentences aloud; class identifies any tense or pronoun errors collaboratively. Teacher notes that reported speech appears naturally in the story when characters retell events — a device worth noticing.

periods.teacher_notes: Task III homework (the six-word table) should have prepared students for the emotional vocabulary in Task IV — draw that link explicitly when presenting the matching activity. The reported-speech transformation is the grammatically heaviest task in this unit; ensure students understand that Wh-question transformation drops the auxiliary and restores standard word order, using the textbook's grammar note as a reference. Any unfinished reported-speech sentences may be completed as self-study.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.116–117): five sentence-completion blanks from a podcast on meditation

periods.activity_title: Listen and Respond: A Podcast on Meditation

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly connects the listening topic to the story: Grandpa's calm, deliberate manner and his advice to Ravi's mother suggest a practised inner composure — today's podcast on meditation explores a discipline that cultivates exactly that quality. Students note two things they already associate with meditation.

Teacher reads the meditation podcast transcript aloud at a natural speaking pace (first listen); students keep pens down and focus on meaning. Teacher then reads it a second time while students fill in the five sentence-completion blanks on p.116–117, writing no more than three exact words per blank.

Teacher reads the transcript a third time at a slightly slower pace; students verify and adjust their answers. Pairs compare; then teacher reads each correct answer aloud for whole-class confirmation, discussing why 'stress management' (not 'relaxation') fits blank 1.

Teacher facilitates a brief discussion: how might regular meditation have helped Ravi during his anxious chase of Grandpa? Students share two or three responses, connecting the podcast's ideas to the story's emotional register.

Teacher recaps the key skill practised: listening for exact words under time pressure. Students note the strategy — listening first for the surrounding context, then for the gap — in their exercise books.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript is a concise teaching monologue on meditation as a yogic practice for relaxation, stress management, emotional well-being, and memory — the memory angle connects neatly to the chapter's 'Vitamin-M' theme and is worth naming for students. A common pitfall is students paraphrasing rather than lifting exact words from the transcript; stress the 'no more than three exact words' constraint during the task. If audio playback is unavailable, teacher reads the transcript at a measured pace as specified.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Speaking Activity (p.117): practise intonation patterns using questions from the story — pairs
Speaking Activity (p.117–118): structured personal narrative presentation — caring for an older person

periods.activity_title: Speaking: Intonation Patterns and Personal Narratives

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the five intonation types (falling for Wh-questions, rising for Yes/No questions, rising for affirmative tag questions, falling for negative tag questions, rise-fall for choice questions) using examples from the Speaking Activity (p.117). Students repeat each type chorally, then locate one example of each type in the story text and practise in pairs.

Students prepare and deliver a brief oral presentation (Speaking Activity, p.117–118) about a personal experience caring for an older person, using the four structured prompts: background, what they learned about themselves, understanding the older person's needs, and insights into the difficulties of aging. Each student speaks for a brief turn; partner listens and notes one specific detail the speaker included effectively.

Three or four volunteers share their presentation with the whole class. Teacher offers formative feedback on intonation, structure, and the specificity of examples — linking back to the story's portrayal of Grandpa's needs and preferences.
Teacher summarises the session: intonation is not decoration but a signal of meaning and relationship. Students note one intonation pattern they found difficult to produce accurately.

periods.teacher_notes: Intonation practice is most effective when students use real sentences from the story rather than invented examples — Grandpa's question 'Did your mother ask you to look after me?' is a natural Yes/No rising pattern, while 'Where are you going?' is a falling Wh-pattern. A common pitfall in the presentation task is students listing facts rather than reflecting; prompt with the scaffolded questions and insist on at least one moment of self-reflection. Time the presentations gently so every student has a spoken turn.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.118): four-paragraph magazine article — 'Our Inspiring Elderly' — plan and first draft

periods.activity_title: Writing Task: Planning and Drafting 'Our Inspiring Elderly'

time_bands.activity: Teacher draws on the character analysis of Grandpa done during the Critical Reflection work — his independence, generosity, and wit — to frame the writing prompt: what makes elderly people inspiring? Students brainstorm two or three examples from the story and from their own experience and note them quickly.

Teacher models the four-paragraph article structure on the board using the given scaffold (p.118): brief introduction, details and examples of how the elderly inspire, how they overcame challenges, concluding comment. Teacher writes two or three sample sentences for paragraph 1 as a model, then hands over to students.

Students write their four-paragraph article independently, including title, name, and grade. Teacher circulates, offering formative guidance on paragraph coherence, the use of specific examples rather than generalities, and appropriate formal register for a school magazine.

Students read their concluding comment aloud to a partner, who identifies whether it rounds off the article or merely stops. Teacher invites one volunteer to share their full draft; class offers one strength and one suggestion.

periods.teacher_notes: The article form requires a formal yet warm register — neither academic nor conversational; use the story's own narrative tone as a touchstone. A common pitfall is students opening with 'The elderly are very important' rather than a hook — encourage a specific anecdote, a surprising fact, or a question. If a student finishes early, prompt them to check that each paragraph has a topic sentence and at least one supporting example.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.118): revise and finalise the four-paragraph magazine article with peer feedback

periods.activity_title: Writing Task: Revising, Peer Feedback, and Final Version

time_bands.activity: Teacher returns to students' draft articles (which they have in front of them) and reads aloud one strong paragraph from a volunteer's work — without naming the student — to illustrate paragraph coherence. The class identifies what makes the paragraph effective.

Students re-read their own draft silently and mark two places where they could add a more specific example or strengthen the link between sentences. Teacher circulates with targeted written feedback on two or three drafts at a time.

Pairs exchange articles and use a simple three-point checklist (clear introduction; specific examples in body; satisfying conclusion) to give structured written feedback on each other's work. Writers then incorporate one peer suggestion before writing the final version.

Students begin writing the final version of their article in their exercise books. Teacher summarises the key moves that lifted the revisions — specificity, a strong conclusion, consistent register — and notes these as transferable writing skills.

periods.teacher_notes: Having drafted the article in the previous sitting, students arrive with a full working text; the value of this sitting lies entirely in the revision and feedback cycle, not in re-explaining the task. A common pitfall is students copying the draft word-for-word rather than genuinely revising; the peer feedback checklist forces at least one substantive change. Articles that are genuinely polished by the end of this sitting may be considered for display or submission to the school magazine.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.119): identify correct image of Grandpa's walking stick — eagle-head brass handle
Learning Beyond the Text (pp.120–125): read 'The Lost Child' by Mulk Raj Anand; discuss attachment, desire, and parental authority with class

periods.activity_title: Beyond the Text: Walking Sticks, Photographs, and 'The Lost Child'

time_bands.activity: Teacher asks students to recall the description of Grandpa's walking stick from the story — mahogany, brass handle, eagle's head — and presents the four images from p.119. Students identify the correct image individually, then discuss: why does the author describe the stick in such detail? What does it signal about Grandpa's character?

Teacher introduces 'The Lost Child' by Mulk Raj Anand (pp.120–125) and reads key passages aloud — the child's suppressed desires at the fair (toys, sweets, balloon, roundabout) and his complete reversal once lost, rejecting every offered comfort in favour of his parents. Students read the remainder silently.

Whole-class discussion guided by two comparison prompts: how does the child's attachment to his parents parallel Grandpa's attachment to his home and independence? And how does Vidya's protective control of Grandpa echo the way the parents restrict the child — with love, but without listening? Students make notes on the comparison.

Teacher draws out the thematic link: both texts — 'Vitamin-M' and 'The Lost Child' — explore what happens when security and autonomy are stripped away from someone who loves them. Students note one sentence articulating this shared theme.

periods.teacher_notes: The eagle-headed walking stick is a carefully chosen character prop — it projects dignity, authority, and an old-fashioned elegance that contradicts the family's perception of Grandpa as helpless; help students read physical details as character signals. Mulk Raj Anand's story is emotionally rich and contrasts desire suppressed by parental authority against the overwhelming bond of attachment when security is lost — prime students to notice that the child stops wanting things the moment he loses his parents. The photograph slideshow task (Task II) is flagged for self-study or a home project.

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.119): memorable family photographs — class slideshow and reflection on memory, identity, and the elderly

periods.activity_title: Beyond the Text: Multilingual Memories and Interdisciplinary Reflection

time_bands.activity: Teacher invites students to share, without physical photographs, a brief spoken description of one memorable family photograph — who is in it, where and when it was taken, and why it is memorable. Three or four volunteers share; teacher notes recurring themes: grandparents at celebrations, homes being left, milestones.

Teacher leads a brief multilingual exploration: what words do students use in their own languages (Tamil, Telugu, Hindi, Kannada, or others) for the bond between grandparent and grandchild? Are there proverbs or folk sayings about elders and memory? Students share in pairs, then offer examples to the class. Teacher notes several on the board.

Students write a reflective paragraph (Learning Beyond the Text, p.119): they describe one memorable family photograph, answering the three prompts — when and where it was taken, who is in it, why it is memorable — and then connect it to one theme from 'Vitamin-M': dignity, memory, intergenerational love, or autonomy.

Two or three students read their reflective paragraph aloud. Teacher closes by returning to the chapter title: what 'vitamin' do families most need to take care of their elderly well? Students offer one-word or one-phrase answers that the teacher records as a final word cloud on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Inviting multilingual proverbs and sayings about elders transforms this into a genuinely interdisciplinary and culturally rooted exploration — students who may be quieter in purely English-language activities often have rich linguistic and cultural knowledge to offer here. A common pitfall is the reflective paragraph becoming a simple description without the thematic connection; insist that the final sentence explicitly names a theme from the story. The chapter's sustained argument — that the elderly deserve dignity, autonomy, and a sharper hearing than they typically get — lands most powerfully when students connect it to their own family stories.

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: Who Needs Vitamin-M? — Integrating Story, Language, and Writing
materials: Students' draft article (notebooks or draft sheets)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens the synthesis by posing three questions on the board — 'What is Vitamin-M really about?', 'Who in this story actually has a memory problem?', and 'What does the story say about aging and dignity?' — and invites students to respond briefly in turn, drawing freely on any part of the chapter they have read: the main story, the extracts, the vocabulary, and 'The Lost Child'.

Class maps the story's key themes on the board together: intergenerational dignity, selective memory, safety vs. autonomy, love expressed obliquely. Teacher draws connections across the chapter — Grandpa's nostalgia for his small-town home, the comedy of errors that demonstrates his competence, the detective-book gift that proves his awareness — showing how each scene contributes to the story's humane argument.

Students complete the draft article 'Our Inspiring Elderly' (Paragraphs 3 and 4 — overcoming challenges and concluding comment), working independently. Those who have already completed the draft review it against the four-paragraph structure and refine the language, replacing generic phrases with specific examples drawn from the story or from their personal caregiving reflections. Teacher circulates, offering brief written or oral feedback on clarity and register.

periods.teacher_notes: This synthesis draws on the full arc of the story — Grandpa's resentment of infantilisation, Ravi's comic surveillance, the birthday twist, and the gift of a detective novel — as well as the vocabulary of movement and sound, the grammar of reported speech, and the comparative themes of 'The Lost Child'. Students need not have covered every task to participate: the chapter's content is now the shared ground, and any student who has read any part of the story has enough to contribute.

items.source_lo: Student analyses character motivation, intergenerational conflict, and narrative irony using a prose short story as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Grandpa's covert birthday outing, Ravi's surveillance comedy, and the birthday-gift twist revealing Grandpa's sharp awareness.
items.item_stem:
Read the following passage from the story and answer the questions below.

1. What does Grandpa's decision to give away his yellow cap to a bald stranger at the barber shop reveal about his character? Identify one specific character trait and support it with this action.
2. Ravi boards a bus chasing the wrong man because of the yellow cap. Explain how the author uses this episode to develop the theme of the tension between protecting someone and respecting their autonomy.
3. The story ends with Grandpa suggesting that Ravi's mother needs Vitamin-M. Analyse the irony in this suggestion, given the opening scene in which Ravi's mother wished someone would invent Vitamin-M for old people.
items.visual_stimulus: Grandpa had another surprise for everyone. He gave a gift to each member of the family. When Ravi's mother assumed the gift was for Ravi's birthday, Grandpa corrected her calmly — it was his own birthday, and he had always given gifts on that day, not received them. He then handed Ravi The Best Detective Stories with a wink, and suggested that it was Ravi's mother who might benefit from Vitamin-M.

expected_elements: Generosity or spontaneous warmth: giving cap to a stranger without hesitation.
Autonomy vs. protection: Ravi's surveillance backfires, showing limits of covert control.
Irony: mother's wish for Vitamin-M is turned back on her by the very person she pitied.
Grandpa's sharp awareness: the detective book gift proves he tracked Ravi all along.
Narrative craft: comic reversal serves the theme — the 'forgetful' elder is most perceptive.

items.item_stem:
You will hear the following passage read aloud twice. Listen carefully and fill in each blank with no more than three exact words you hear.

1. Meditation is commonly described as a yogic practice used for relaxation and ___.
2. During meditation, thoughts that cause stress are removed, resulting in an enhanced state of well-being both physically and ___.
3. After a session of meditation, a person gains ___ on stressful situations.
4. Practising meditation regularly is said to reduce negative emotions and increase ___.
5. Daily meditation is described as beneficial for managing ___ with ease.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. stress management. 2. emotionally. 3. a new perspective. 4. self-awareness. 5. exam-related pressure (or: challenges).

items.source_lo: Student delivers a structured personal narrative using appropriate intonation and reflective content to an audience.
items.source_context: Personal experience of caring for an older person, structured around background, self-reflection, the person's needs, and insights into aging.
items.item_stem: Deliver a structured oral presentation of three to four minutes on the following topic: Describe a real or imagined experience in which you spent a day helping an elderly person complete a task they found difficult — for example, navigating a market, filling a form, or attending a medical appointment. In your presentation, address all four points: (1) the background and who the person was; (2) what specific challenges the task posed for them; (3) what you learned about the person's needs and preferences; (4) how the experience changed your understanding of what it means to grow old with dignity. Use rising intonation when asking a rhetorical question and falling intonation when making a concluding statement.

expected_elements: Clear background: names person, context, and specific task undertaken.
Specific challenges described with empathy, not pity or condescension.
Reflection on the person's preferences, showing genuine listening.
Insight into dignity and aging — goes beyond surface observation.
Correct intonation on at least one rhetorical question and one concluding statement.

items.source_lo: Student writes a structured four-paragraph magazine article using a formal register, specific examples, and a cohesive argument.
items.source_context: An elderly resident of a multi-generational housing complex who continues to mentor young neighbours through traditional crafts.
items.item_stem: You are a student reporter for your school magazine. Write a four-paragraph article titled 'Still Teaching Us' about an elderly resident of a multi-generational housing complex who mentors young neighbours through traditional crafts such as pottery, weaving, or kite-making. Your article must include: Paragraph 1 — a brief, engaging introduction that draws the reader in; Paragraph 2 — specific details and examples of how this person mentors and inspires the young; Paragraph 3 — the challenges of aging they have overcome and the impact their persistence has had; Paragraph 4 — a concluding comment that connects their story to a broader reflection on intergenerational respect. Write your name and grade below the title. Use a formal yet warm register appropriate for a school magazine.

expected_elements: Opening paragraph hooks the reader with a specific image or anecdote.
Body paragraphs use named, specific examples — not vague generalisations.
Paragraph on challenges shows empathy and links persistence to inspiration.
Conclusion offers a broader reflection, not merely a summary.
Formal yet warm register maintained consistently; correct paragraph structure.

items.source_lo: Student classifies domain vocabulary, uses contextual synonyms, applies prepositions precisely, and transforms direct questions into reported speech.
items.source_context: Movement and sound words from the chase sequence; prepositions of place; interrogative sentence types; reported speech from story dialogues.
items.item_stem:
Part A — Reported Speech Transformation
Ravi's mother spoke to Ravi before leaving for work. Convert the following direct speech sentences into reported speech. Write the complete transformed sentence for each.
1. She said to Ravi, "Do not let Grandpa go out alone today."
2. She asked him, "Will you stay at home with Grandpa?"
3. She warned him, "Where will you go if something happens to him?"

Part B — Prepositions
Choose the correct preposition from the brackets and fill in each blank.
4. Ravi crouched ___ the elephant-shaped bush, hoping Grandpa would not notice him. (behind / across / beside)
5. Grandpa walked ___ the road and entered the barber's shop calmly. (among / across / along)
6. A shadow fell ___ Ravi as he hid near the banyan tree. (over / beside / between)

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Part A: 1. She told Ravi not to let Grandpa go out alone that day. 2. She asked him whether he would stay at home with Grandpa. 3. She asked him where he would go if something happened to him. Part B: 4. behind. 5. across. 6. over.

items.source_lo: Student makes thematic comparisons across texts and connects personal cultural memory to literary themes through reflective writing and multilingual exploration.
items.source_context: Mulk Raj Anand's 'The Lost Child' — attachment, suppressed desire, and the bond of security — compared with the intergenerational themes of Vitamin-M.
items.item_stem: In 'The Lost Child' by Mulk Raj Anand, a young child eagerly desires toys, sweets, and a ride on the roundabout throughout the spring festival, but restrains himself knowing his parents will refuse. Once separated from his parents, he rejects every one of these same things offered by a kind stranger, crying only for his mother and father. In 'Vitamin-M', Grandpa deeply desires his independence, his garden, and the freedom to go to the tea stall — comforts his family has removed for his own safety. Write a comparative response of two paragraphs addressing the following: (1) How does the experience of losing security or freedom change what each character — the child and Grandpa — truly values? (2) What does each text suggest about the relationship between love and control in families? Use specific details from both texts to support your comparison.

expected_elements: Child values parents over objects once security is lost; Grandpa values autonomy and dignity over comfort.
Both texts show that what is withheld becomes most precious — desire sharpened by deprivation.
Love and control are intertwined in both families — protective intent does not erase the cost.
Specific textual details cited from each story to support claims.
Comparison is analytical, not merely a list of similarities and differences.
